headline: A 27B Team Matches a 1.6-Trillion-Parameter Giant at a fraction of the token cost
summary: An open-source model “technical committee” beats a 1.6T cloud flagship by 15 percentage points on real engineering tasks, without stacking more parameters or burning more cash.
details: AI models often get stuck in repetitive loops on complex engineering tasks, wasting tokens and failing to solve issues. This problem is common in real-world AI coding deployments, where models can spin in circles without external intervention.

The industry has seen approaches like OpenRouter's Fusion and Hermes' Mixture of Agents to address this. The new Fusion-MOA system takes a counterintuitive approach: a single GPU server with a 27B open-source model leading, supported by other models for consultations.

This setup achieved a 50% pass rate on real-world terminal engineering tasks. It outperformed a 295-billion-parameter cloud flagship and beat a 1.6-trillion-parameter giant by 15 percentage points, all while consuming a small fraction of their tokens.

The "Jagged Frontier" concept highlights that AI capabilities are inconsistent; a model can excel in one area and fail in another. Real engineering issues require diverse abilities like reading legacy code, debugging error logs, and reasoning about changes.

Fusion-MOA's core principle is not about finding the single strongest model, but about organizing models smartly. It treats models as units with clearly defined responsibilities, service endpoints, execution policies, and traceable records, rather than just adding more headcount.

The current general-purpose Fusion-MOA profile consists of one Executor and three read-only Analysts. These roles correspond to system-level privileges, with the Client/Agent handling external task state and the Gateway validating interfaces and detecting stalls.

headline_marked: [[Meta AI achieves perfect score]] on a 2026 Physics Olympiad exam that was already solved
headline: Meta AI achieves perfect score on a 2026 Physics Olympiad exam that was already solved
summary: Meta's AI division announced a perfect score on the theoretical part of the 2026 Asian Physics Olympiad. This highlights formal reasoning, but experts note such exams don't test real-world ambiguity.
details: Meta AI announced a perfect score on the theoretical section of the 2026 Asian Physics Olympiad. This achievement, shared by Meta's official AI division, demonstrates the model's capability for flawless, long chains of verifiable deductions.

Scientific Olympiads are highly bounded exercises with complete statements, sufficient data, and known solutions. This structure makes them reliable measures of formal reasoning but not of autonomy or real-world problem framing.

In contrast, typical work tasks involve ambiguous requests, missing data, and multiple potential solutions. AI agents often struggle here, not with calculation, but with defining the problem itself, an error not addressed by Olympiad formats.

The perfect score was specifically for the *theoretical* exam. Physics Olympiads also include an experimental component where real-world variables and manipulation can introduce challenges, a scope not covered by this achievement.

Similar achievements have been reported before, with Gemini Deep Think and OpenAI claiming high scores on math Olympiads. A key question remains about whether these models are truly reconstructing solutions or memorizing them from widely available online sources.

Meta states its model competed without external tools, code execution, or internet search, which addresses part of the memorization concern. However, further verifiable details on the exact protocol and training data are still awaited.

While such scores demonstrate strong long-chain reasoning, they don't reflect a model's ability to handle vague requests or unstructured problems. This gap remains a major obstacle for deploying AI agents effectively in complex enterprise environments.
